primer.text: Rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are consumed or products formed, in mol dm-3 s-1. This note defines rate, shows how concentration data reveal a proportional relationship between rate and concentration, and introduces the rate equation, where experimentally determined orders and a rate constant tie reactant concentrations to rate. Products and catalysts may appear; intermediates never do.

modules.title: Defining the rate of reaction
modules.opening: Kinetics begins with a definition: the rate of reaction is how quickly a reactant is consumed or a product appears, per unit time. This lesson fixes the units, lists the physical changes a chemist can watch to follow a reaction, and sets up the model reaction used throughout the topic.
keyPoints: Rate of reaction tracks how fast a reactant is used up or a product forms, expressed as a concentration change per unit time with units mol dm-3 s-1.
Rate can be followed by measuring mass lost, gas volume produced, colour or pH change, or electrical conductivity as time passes.
Rate is calculated as concentration change divided by the time interval over which that change happens.
The model reaction D (aq) to E (aq) plus F (g) lets rates be tabulated at several concentrations of D.

low.restatement: Rate is a concentration change divided by time, tracked through any property that moves with concentration such as mass, volume, colour, pH or conductivity.
low.analogy: A bathroom scale tells you how fast a bathtub drains only if you weigh it every few seconds; each weighing is one rate data point.
low.examPointer: Quote the units mol dm-3 s-1 whenever you state a rate - examiners check them.

medium.restatement: Because rate compares two quantities, concentration and time, any measurable stand-in for concentration works; the property only needs to change smoothly as the reaction proceeds.
medium.analogy: Watching a kettle cool: you cannot read temperature directly, but the steam thins, the glass mist fades and the sound softens - each is a proxy for the falling temperature.
medium.examPointer: If asked how to follow a given reaction, pick the property that changes and justify the choice from the state symbols.

modules.title: From concentration data to the rate equation
modules.opening: Tabulated rates for the model reaction show rate rising in step with the concentration of D. That proportionality condenses into the rate expression rate = k[D], and the general rate equation rate = k[A]^m[B]^n follows. This lesson separates what rate equations may contain from what they may not.
keyPoints: The tabulated data for D show rate and concentration rising together, a directly proportional relationship.
Proportionality is written as the rate expression rate proportional to [D], or rate = k[D], where k is the rate constant.
For A plus B giving C plus D the general rate equation is rate = k[A]^m[B]^n with orders m and n.
Orders must be found by experiment; stoichiometric coefficients never fix them.
Products and catalysts may appear in a rate equation, but intermediates do not.

low.restatement: Doubling [D] doubles the rate, so rate = k[D]; in general rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, with the powers found only from experiments.
low.analogy: A volume dial on a hose: turn it twice as far and twice as much water flows - the dial setting and flow are proportional, like [D] and rate here.
low.examPointer: State plainly that rate equations come from experiment, never from the balancing numbers.

medium.restatement: The rate constant k is the proportionality glue between concentration and rate; the powers m and n are the orders that experiments reveal, not the balancing numbers that the equation happens to carry.
medium.analogy: A recipe that scales: the serving count scales with ingredients (the proportional part), but only tasting the dish tells you which ingredient dominates the flavour (the experimental orders).
medium.examPointer: If an option claims orders can be read from the stoichiometric equation, reject it outright - that is the classic trap.

glossary.definition: How quickly a reactant is used up or a product forms, expressed as a concentration change per unit time, in mol dm-3 s-1.
The expression rate = k[A]^m[B]^n linking rate to reactant concentrations raised to experimentally determined powers.
The proportionality factor k in a rate equation, fixed for a given reaction at a given temperature.
A species made and consumed within a mechanism that never appears in the rate equation.
